295.title: Rabi'a of Basra
295.hook: Rabi'a of Basra, who prayed to love Allah for Himself, not for heaven or fear of hell
295.howItsDone: Sufis honor Rabi'a of Basra for placing pure love of God at the center of the path, and her attributed sayings are still taught in Sufi circles and recited in poetry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ihsan, from the hadith of Jibril: to worship as though you see Him, and if you don't, He sees you. Your line was as though you see him. What did you do beautifully? Day two hundred ninety-five.

Why does anyone do good? For love. For the thanks, the good feeling, the reputation. For fear of what happens if they don't. Usually it's a mix. Basra, in southern Iraq, in the generations after the Prophet. People tell a story about a woman walking through the city with a torch in one hand and a bucket of water in the other. Someone stops her and asks what she's doing. Today, her answer, and her name.
screen: `WHY DO YOU DO GOOD?` → `BASRA, IN SOUTHERN IRAQ.` → `A TORCH AND A BUCKET.`

segments.voice: The woman is Rabi'a al-'Adawiyya, Rabi'a of Basra, who died, tradition says, around the year 800. In the story, she says: I want to set fire to paradise and pour water on the fires of hell, so that both veils are gone, and people worship God not out of hope for reward or fear of punishment, but for His own sake. It's a story people tell, not a sourced report. And here we need to be honest about the sources. Rabi'a left no writings. Much of what's told about her comes from writers who lived long after her, above all the Persian poet Farid al-Din 'Attar, writing centuries later. Tradition says she was born poor, was enslaved as a girl, and was freed because her master saw a light over her while she prayed at night. Historians can't confirm those details. What's consistent across the sources is the center of her teaching: love. Mahabbah. There's a prayer attributed to her, in the old Sufi books, that runs roughly like this: if I worship You out of fear of hell, then burn me in it; if I worship You hoping for paradise, then shut me out of it; but if I worship You for Your own sake, then don't hold back Your eternal beauty from me. The Qur'an speaks of people whom God loves and who love Him. Rabi'a, as she's remembered, made that love the center. She isn't saying heaven and hell don't matter; Muslims hold that they're real. She's asking what's underneath. Love for its own sake.
screen: `A STORY: FIRE ON PARADISE, WATER ON HELL.` · `NO WRITINGS; LATER BIOGRAPHIES.` · `MAHABBAH — LOVE.` · `FOR YOUR OWN SAKE.` · then, large: `LOVE FOR ITS OWN SAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one good thing with no reward. Sit, and breathe. Think of a small kindness you could do today that nobody will ever know was you. Paying for a stranger's coffee. Picking up litter on a street you'll never walk again. Praying for someone who doesn't know you exist. Choose it now. Notice the part of you that wants credit, and just smile at it. If you pray, you can ask to love for its own sake. The bell holds the time.
Mahabbah. Love — the center of Rabi'a of Basra's teaching, worshiping God for His own sake alone. Today's word.
Your line: love for its own sake. Today, do one good thing in secret, and don't tell anyone, not even later. Day two hundred ninety-five.

296.title: Junayd of Baghdad
296.hook: Junayd of Baghdad, the sober master, who taught the path must hold to the Qur'an and sunnah
296.howItsDone: Many Sufi orders trace their teaching through Junayd and follow his insistence that the inner path stay within the Qur'an, the sunnah and the law; his letters and sayings are studied in Sufi handbooks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabi'a of Basra, with a torch for paradise and water for hell, in the story people tell of mahabbah. Your line was love for its own sake. Did you do one good thing in secret? Day two hundred ninety-six.

Everyone knows someone who falls in love hard. They stop sleeping, they write poems at two in the morning, they say things they'd never say sober. And everyone knows someone who loves just as deeply and still shows up to work on time, pays the rent and remembers your birthday. Both are real love. Early Sufis had the same two temperaments. Some were famous for their ecstasy, for wild sayings in moments of overwhelming nearness to God. And in Baghdad, around the year 900, there was a master known for the other kind. Later Sufis called him sayyid al-ta'ifa, the master of the whole group. Today, the sober one.
screen: `TWO KINDS OF LOVE.` → `ECSTASY, OR STEADINESS.` → `BAGHDAD, AROUND 900.`

segments.voice: His name was Abu al-Qasim al-Junayd, and he died in Baghdad around the year 910. He'd learned the path from his uncle, a Sufi teacher named Sari al-Saqati, and he'd also studied the law, deeply. Later writers used two words for the two temperaments on the path. Sukr: intoxication, being overwhelmed, carried away. And sahw: sobriety, coming back to yourself. Junayd is remembered as the great master of sobriety. For him, the highest point wasn't getting lost in ecstasy and staying there. It was being drawn close to God and then coming back, awake, to live an ordinary life of prayer, work and kindness, with that nearness still inside. His best-known rule, as the early Sufi handbooks report it, goes roughly like this: our knowledge is tied to the Qur'an and the sunnah, and whoever hasn't learned the Qur'an and written down hadith shouldn't be followed in this path. In other words: no inner experience gets to overrule the Book. That made him a bridge. Scholars of the law who distrusted Sufis could respect Junayd, and many later Sufi chains of teachers pass through his name. Some of the ecstatic Sufis said things that shocked their neighbors, and there were real conflicts over it. Junayd's way was careful: love God with everything, and keep your feet on the ground of the law. Sober love.
screen: `SARI'S NEPHEW, AND A SCHOLAR OF LAW.` · `SUKR AND SAHW — DRUNK AND SOBER.` · `TIED TO THE QUR'AN AND SUNNAH.` · `A BRIDGE BETWEEN LAW AND LOVE.` · then, large: `SOBER LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one rule and one prayer. Sit, and breathe. Choose one small rule you'll keep today, steady and unglamorous: no phone at the table, on time for one thing, a promise kept. Then choose one moment of prayer or stillness you'll keep too: a prayer at its time, if you pray, or a quiet minute, if you don't. One for the feet, one for the heart. Hold both in mind now. The bell holds the time.
Sahw. Sobriety, coming back to yourself after being drawn near to God — the mark of Junayd of Baghdad's path. Today's word.
Your line: sober love. Today, when a big feeling rises, let it be real, and then come back and do the next ordinary thing well. Day two hundred ninety-six.

297.title: Al-Ghazali's crisis
297.hook: the famous scholar leaves his post in doubt and finds the living path (Deliverance from Error)
297.howItsDone: Al-Ghazali's Revival of the Religious Sciences is still read in mosques and study circles, and his account of his crisis is often taught as a model of honest searching within the faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Junayd of Baghdad, the master of sahw, sobriety, who tied the inner path to the Qur'an and the sunnah. Your line was sober love. Did you come back and do the next ordinary thing well? Day two hundred ninety-seven.

A professor at the top of his field. Students crowding his lectures, rulers asking his opinion, his books read everywhere. And one day he stands up to teach, and can't speak. His tongue won't move. He can't eat. The doctors examine him and say it isn't his body; it's something in his heart. That happened in Baghdad, in the year 1095, to a celebrated scholar. He wrote about it himself, later, in a short book about his search for certainty. Today, his crisis.
screen: `AT THE TOP OF HIS FIELD.` → `HE STANDS TO TEACH, AND CAN'T.` → `BAGHDAD, 1095.`

segments.voice: His name was Abu Hamid al-Ghazali. He was a master of law, theology and philosophy, and he taught at the Nizamiyya, the great college of Baghdad. In his book, called Deliverance from Error, he says he'd started doubting how anyone can know anything for certain, and he went through every school he could find: the theologians, the philosophers, the ones who claimed secret teachers. Finally he turned to the Sufis, read their books, and understood them. And he realized something. He could explain their path perfectly, and he hadn't walked a single step of it. He gives an example. There's a difference, he says, between knowing the definition of health and being healthy, between knowing what makes a person full and actually being full. The Sufi word for the second kind of knowing is dhawq, tasting. As if he could describe honey without ever having tasted it. And he saw that his fame, his salary and his reputation were the very things holding him back. That's when his tongue stopped. So he gave away his wealth, except what his family needed, and left Baghdad quietly. He spent years traveling, to Damascus, Jerusalem and the holy cities, praying, keeping silent, practicing. In those years he wrote his great work, the Revival of the Religious Sciences, joining the law and the inner path in one book. Later Muslims called him Hujjat al-Islam, the proof of Islam. It started with admitting a doubt. Knowing is not tasting.
screen: `DELIVERANCE FROM ERROR.` · `HE COULD EXPLAIN IT, NOT WALK IT.` · `DHAWQ — TASTING.` · `HE GAVE IT UP AND LEFT.` · then, large: `KNOWING IS NOT TASTING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: admit one doubt honestly. Sit, and breathe. Think of something you're supposed to be sure of, about faith, your work, a relationship, yourself, and let yourself notice where you're actually unsure. Don't solve it. Don't panic. Al-Ghazali's doubt was the door, not the end. Just name it plainly to yourself. If you pray, you can bring the doubt to God as it is. If you don't, just let it sit beside you without arguing. The bell holds the time.
Al-Ghazali's crisis. The great scholar who lost his voice, left his post, and went looking to taste what he knew. Today's word.
Your line: knowing is not tasting. Today, pick one thing you know a lot about and actually do it, instead of explaining it. Day two hundred ninety-seven.

298.title: Rumi of Konya
298.hook: Jalal al-Din Rumi, scholar of Konya, whose life turns when he meets Shams of Tabriz
298.howItsDone: Muslims across Turkey, Iran, Central and South Asia read Rumi's Masnavi as a work of Islamic spirituality, and every December many gather in Konya to mark the night of his death, which his followers call his wedding night with God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Ghazali's crisis: the great scholar who could explain the path and hadn't tasted it. Your line was knowing is not tasting. What did you do instead of explain? Day two hundred ninety-eight.

His name turns up on mugs, posters and wedding invitations. But the man behind the quotes wasn't a greeting-card poet. He was a Muslim scholar, a preacher and a teacher of the law, in a city in the middle of what's now Turkey. He led prayers. He taught students. He was respected and settled. And then a wandering stranger walked into his life, and the scholar's life turned. Today, the scholar of Konya, and the meeting.
screen: `THE NAME ON THE MUG.` → `A SCHOLAR, A PREACHER, A TEACHER.` → `THEN A STRANGER ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Jalal al-Din Muhammad was born, by the usual account, in 1207, in the eastern Persian-speaking world, around Balkh. When he was a boy, his family moved west, just ahead of the Mongol invasions, and settled in Konya, in Anatolia. That region was called Rum, after the old Roman lands, and that's where his name comes from: Rumi, the one from Rum. Muslims often call him Mawlana, our master. His father was a preacher and scholar, and when his father died, Rumi took over his teaching. Then, in 1244, a wandering dervish named Shams, from Tabriz, arrived in Konya. The stories of their first meeting are many, and they're later legends; nobody knows exactly what happened. What's certain is what followed. The two became inseparable, talking for days on end. Rumi's students grew jealous. Shams left, came back, and then, a few years later, disappeared for good. Some said he was killed; the sources are unsure. Rumi searched for him and didn't find him. And out of that grief, the scholar became a poet. He composed thousands of verses of love poetry, and he named the collection after Shams. Later he dictated his great work, the Masnavi, full of stories and verses of the Qur'an. The Rumi on the mug is often stripped of all that. The early accounts describe a man who kept the prayers and the fasts, and his Masnavi draws on the Qur'an again and again. It all turned on one friend. The meeting.
screen: `BORN 1207, SETTLED IN KONYA.` · `RUMI — THE ONE FROM RUM.` · `SHAMS OF TABRIZ, 1244.` · `THE SCHOLAR BECOMES A POET.` · then, large: `THE MEETING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a friend who changed you. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who turned your life in a new direction. A teacher, a friend, a stranger for one afternoon, someone who asked the question nobody else asked. Picture their face. Remember what you were like before, and after. If they're alive, consider telling them. If they're gone, hold them for a moment with thanks. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Mawlana. Our master — the title given to Rumi of Konya, the scholar whose meeting with Shams of Tabriz turned him into a poet. Today's word.
Your line: the meeting. Today, send one message to someone who changed you, and tell them how. Day two hundred ninety-eight.

299.title: The reed flute
299.hook: the Masnavi opens with a reed cut from its reed-bed, crying to return (Masnavi 1, opening)
299.howItsDone: Readers of the Masnavi often begin with its opening lines, the Song of the Reed, which are recited and sung in Persian; the ney is played in the Mevlevi ceremony and in Sufi gatherings across Turkey, Iran and beyond.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mawlana, Rumi of Konya, the scholar whose life turned when Shams of Tabriz walked in. Your line was the meeting. Did you tell someone how they changed you? Day two hundred ninety-nine.

Have you ever heard a sound that made you homesick for a place you couldn't name? A train horn at night. A song from a street you'll never walk again. A flute somewhere in a movie that makes your chest ache for no reason. Rumi's great poem, the Masnavi, runs to six books. And the very first thing it asks you to do isn't to believe or to study. It's to listen. To one instrument: the ney, the reed flute of Persia and Turkey, breathy and low, a sound like someone sighing. Today, the reed flute.
screen: `HOMESICK FOR A NAMELESS PLACE.` → `A LONG POEM IN SIX BOOKS.` → `THE FIRST WORD: LISTEN.`

segments.voice: In E. H. Whinfield's Victorian English translation, the Masnavi begins: "Hearken to the reed-flute, how it complains." The reed goes on to tell its story. It was cut from the reed bed where it grew, and ever since, it cries. Its cry, it says, has made men and women moan, because the song is a longing to go back. Think about how a ney is made. You cut a reed from the marsh. You hollow it out, burn holes in it, and it's empty inside. And only because it's empty and cut off can breath pass through it and make music. The reed's cry isn't a malfunction. It's the song. Rumi's readers have understood the reed as the human soul. It came from God, it's been cut off and sent into the world, and its ache, a homesickness for a place it can't name, is the soul remembering where it came from. The Qur'an has a line Muslims say when something is lost, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Readers have heard the reed as that verse set to music. There's a second layer. A flute doesn't play itself. Someone breathes through it. Sufis read that as: the song is the player's, not the reed's. The reed's only job is to be hollow and let the breath through. That's why the Masnavi starts with listening. Before any story or teaching, the poem asks for an ear.
screen: `HEARKEN TO THE REED-FLUTE.` · `CUT FROM THE REED BED.` · `HOLLOW, SO BREATH CAN PASS.` · `UNTO HIM WE ARE RETURNING.` · then, large: `LISTEN TO THE REED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hum one long note. Sit comfortably. Breathe in slowly, all the way down. Then, on the out-breath, hum one low, long note, as long as it lasts, and feel it in your chest and your face. Let yourself be hollow, like the reed, and let the breath do the work. Do it two or three times, then sit in the quiet after the sound. If you pray, you can let the note carry your longing to God. The bell holds the time.
Ney. The reed flute that opens Rumi's Masnavi, cut from its reed bed, crying to go home. Today's word.
Your line: listen to the reed. Today, when a sound or a song makes you ache, don't skip it. Listen to the end, and ask what it's homesick for. Day two hundred ninety-nine.

screen: `DAY 299 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE ELEPHANT IN THE DARK.`

300.title: The elephant in the dark
300.hook: people feel an elephant in a dark room, and each describes a different thing (Masnavi 3)
300.howItsDone: The elephant in the dark is a story from the Masnavi taught in Sufi circles and schools as a lesson in the limits of the senses and the need for the inner light that comes from God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ney, the reed flute, cut from its reed bed and crying to go home. Your line was listen to the reed. What sound made you ache? Day three hundred. Three hundred days on the path.

Two people describe the same event, the same boss, the same family dinner, and it sounds like they were at two different places. Each one is completely sure. Each one is partly right. And nobody's listening. In the third book of the Masnavi, Rumi tells a short story. Some people from India bring an elephant to a town where nobody has ever seen one, and they keep it in a dark house. People are curious, and they file in, one by one, to find out what an elephant is. It's too dark to see anything. So they reach out with their hands. Today, the elephant in the dark.
screen: `SAME EVENT, TWO STORIES.` → `AN ELEPHANT IN A DARK HOUSE.` → `THEY REACH OUT WITH THEIR HANDS.`

segments.voice: One man's hand lands on the trunk, and he comes out and says: an elephant is like a water pipe. Another touches an ear: no, it's like a fan. Another feels a leg: it's a pillar. Another runs his palm along its back: it's like a throne. Each of them is describing something real. Each of them is wrong about the elephant. And Rumi adds the line the story turns on: if each of them had held a candle, their differences would have gone away. Rumi didn't invent the story. An older Persian poet, Sana'i, told a version, and a version was told in India centuries before either of them. It traveled far. But notice what Rumi does with it. He says the eye of the senses is like the palm of a hand: the palm can't hold the whole of the elephant. The problem isn't that the people are stupid, or lying. It's that they're in the dark, and they're trusting a hand to do the work of a light. For Rumi, the candle is the light that comes from God, the light of an inner sight that sees the whole. Readers have used the story in many ways since. At the very least, it asks for some humility: the thing you're touching is real, and it's probably not the whole elephant. A candle would help.
screen: `A PIPE, A FAN, A PILLAR, A THRONE.` · `EACH REAL, EACH WRONG.` · `THE PALM CAN'T HOLD THE WHOLE.` · `THE CANDLE IS A LIGHT FROM GOD.` · then, large: `A CANDLE WOULD HELP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hear someone's view without arguing. Sit, and breathe. Think of a person you disagree with, about something small or something big. Picture them in the dark room, describing the part of the elephant they're touching. What is their hand on? What's real in what they're saying? Just imagine listening to them to the end, without preparing your answer. If you pray, you can ask for light, for both of you. The bell holds the time.
Sham'. A candle — the light that, Rumi says, would have let each one touching the elephant in the dark see the whole. Today's word.
Your line: a candle would help. Today, in one disagreement, ask one real question about what the other person is touching before you say what you're touching. Day three hundred.

301.title: Every state a guest
301.hook: Rumi teaches that every state of the heart comes to teach and then leaves
301.howItsDone: Sufi teachers distinguish passing states, ahwal, from lasting stations, maqamat, and teach students to receive each state with patience and gratitude without clinging to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the elephant in the dark: a pipe, a fan, a pillar, a throne, each one real and none of them whole — needing sham', a candle. Your line was a candle would help. Whose view did you hear to the end? Day three hundred one, the end of the week.

Some mornings you wake up and a mood is already sitting at the kitchen table. Nobody invited it. Dread about a meeting. A heaviness with no reason. Sometimes it's a good one, a lightness you can't explain. And our first instinct, with the hard ones, is to shove them out the door, or to decide that this is who we are now, forever. Rumi had another idea. You may have seen a poem shared online about the human being as a guest house. That popular English poem is a modern, free version. The older Persian lines are in the fifth book of the Masnavi. Today, the guests.
screen: `A MOOD AT THE KITCHEN TABLE.` → `SHOVE IT OUT, OR MOVE IT IN?` → `THE FIFTH BOOK OF THE MASNAVI.`

segments.voice: Rumi pictures the thoughts and feelings that arrive in you as guests. Each day, at every moment, he says, a new one comes into the heart. Treat each one with honor, even the sad ones, because a guest comes from somewhere, and each one is sent. A sorrow may be clearing out the house so that a new joy can move in. And guests don't stay. They teach what they came to teach, and then they leave. Sufis had words for this long before Rumi. A hal is a state: a mood of the heart that comes and goes, like longing, or fear, or joy, or nearness to God. A maqam is a station: something you work for and that stays, like patience or trust. The teachers said you can't hold on to a state, and you shouldn't try. It's a gift, and it moves on. The Qur'an has a line in the same spirit, revealed after the hard day at Uhud: days like these, it says, are passed around among people, turn by turn. Good days and hard days each take their turn, and none of them moves in for good. And this has been a week of guests on the path: Rabi'a and love for its own sake, Junayd and sober love, al-Ghazali, for whom knowing is not tasting, Rumi and the meeting, the reed, the elephant and the candle. Each came, taught, and moved on to make room for the next. Every state is a guest.
screen: `EVERY MOMENT, A NEW GUEST.` · `SORROW CLEARS THE HOUSE.` · `HAL COMES AND GOES; MAQAM STAYS.` · `DAYS TAKE TURNS AMONG PEOPLE.` · then, large: `EVERY STATE IS A GUEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome one hard feeling. Sit, and breathe. Notice what's here right now. Maybe tiredness, worry, irritation, sadness. Pick one. Instead of pushing it away, imagine opening the door to it, like a guest. Where does it sit in your body? What might it have come to tell you? You don't have to agree with it. Just treat it with courtesy, and remember it's not moving in. If you pray, you can ask God what the guest was sent to teach. The bell holds the time.
Hal. A state of the heart that comes and goes — Rumi's picture of every mood as a guest that teaches, then leaves. Today's word.
Your line: every state is a guest. Today, when a hard mood arrives, greet it, ask what it came for, and remember it isn't staying. Day three hundred one.

fork.setup: you wake up and sorrow is already sitting at the kitchen table. what does Rumi say to do?
options: throw it out the door.
treat it as a guest, with honor, because it was sent.
decide it's who you are now.
fork.reveal: honor the guest, even a sad one: it may be clearing the house for a new joy, and it won't stay.

original.note: Arabic: a state of the heart that comes and goes; plural ahwal. contrasted with maqam, a lasting station.

trapdoor: what you thought: be positive about bad moods.
what it means: receive each state with courtesy, learn from it, and let it go; it was sent, and it won't stay.
what a scholar hears: the guest-house passage in Masnavi Book 5, and the classical Sufi distinction between hal and maqam, found in al-Qushayri's Risala.
